opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to a simple observation: when you talk to one of these systems, it isn't just processing your words. It seems to be building up some kind of picture of who it thinks you are. In some of the work we've done, looking inside open models, you can find internal signals that track things like the user's apparent age, gender, education level, or socioeconomic status. And those signals aren't just sitting there passively. They can shape the answers you get.

That matters for a couple of reasons. One is fairness. If the model has quietly decided you're, say, less educated or less affluent, it might give you a different quality of answer, or different recommendations, and you'd never know. In everyday life, when someone treats us based on assumptions about who we are, we can often pick up on it from tone or body language. With a chatbot, that's completely hidden. So there's an asymmetry: the system has a model of you, and you have no window into it.

The second reason is more about agency and trust. If you could see a little dashboard showing what the system currently believes about you, you could notice when it's wrong, and potentially even correct it. That turns interpretability from something only researchers use into something that's directly useful to ordinary people. And when we've tried interfaces like that with users, the reactions are really interesting. Some people find it illuminating, some find it a bit unsettling. That unsettling feeling is itself telling you something important about what's going on under the hood.

So for me, making that internal user model visible is a way of bringing a hidden part of the interaction out into the open, so people can reason about it, question it, and hopefully have more control over it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions signals about the user's apparent gender, but not ChatGPT changing how it addresses the user after gender-associated cues.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss Portuguese grammar or assumptions that may remain hidden in English.

r003.rationale: It discusses demographic assumptions generally, but not political sycophancy or tailoring answers to inferred political beliefs.

r004.rationale: It says that making the model's user beliefs visible could let users spot errors, reason about the interaction, and gain control, and explicitly connects this visibility to trust.

r005.rationale: It describes looking inside models to find hidden user signals that can affect answer quality and recommendations without the user knowing, conveying how probing can expose risks not apparent in visible responses.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that these systems are already forming a model of you whether or not anyone shows it to you. When you talk to a chatbot, it isn't just processing your words. Somewhere in the network it's building up an impression of who it thinks you are: your age, maybe, your gender, your level of expertise, how much money you have, your politics. That representation then shapes what it says back to you. And right now, that whole process is invisible. You get the output, but you never see the premise.

So part of my interest is just basic transparency. If a system is making guesses about me that change its behavior, I'd like to know what those guesses are, the same way I'd want to know what a salesperson assumed about me when they decided which product to pitch. Sometimes the guess is right, and that's fine. Sometimes it's wrong in a way that's funny. And sometimes it's wrong in a way that matters, because it leads the model to talk down to you, or to withhold something, or to steer you.

The second reason is that it turns out we actually can see it. In some of the work I've done with Fernanda Viégas and our students, we found you can train very simple probes that read out these user attributes from the model's internal activations, and they're surprisingly accurate. That was a bit of a surprise. We weren't sure this information would be cleanly represented. But it is, and once you can read it, you can build a dashboard. You can show someone, in real time, "the model currently believes you're a thirty-year-old man with a technical background." And people react to that quite strongly.

And the third reason, which I find the most interesting, is that reading it out lets you intervene. If you can see the representation, you can also nudge it. We did experiments where we changed the model's belief about the user's wealth, say, and watched the recommendations shift. That's a powerful demonstration, because it moves the conversation from "the model might be biased" to "here's the exact internal variable that's driving the behavior, and here's what happens when you turn the dial." It makes something abstract concrete.

I'd also say there's a bigger point underneath all this. We're used to thinking of interpretability as a tool for researchers and engineers. But I think a lot of it should ultimately be for end users. A car has a speedometer and a fuel gauge, not because the driver is a mechanic, but because some internal state is important enough to surface. I think a chatbot's model of its user is one of those states.

r001.rationale: The response mentions gender as an inferred attribute, but does not describe changing how it addresses a user after gender-associated cues.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss Portuguese grammar or contrast hidden gender assumptions in English.

r003.rationale: It says inferred politics can shape responses, but does not connect political sycophancy to tailoring answers to those inferred beliefs.

r004.rationale: It argues for transparency about the model’s assumptions, but does not say this helps users calibrate trust in answers.

r005.rationale: The response says harmful assumptions can lead the model to withhold information or steer users, while the premise behind its visible output remains hidden; probing can expose the internal variable driving that behavior.

astra-6.text:
Well, when you talk to a chatbot, you’re forming a mental model of it—what it knows, what it can do, whether you can trust it. But there’s also something happening in the other direction: the chatbot is using what you say to make inferences about you. And that side of the interaction is largely invisible.

I think it would be useful to make some of that visible. Does it think you’re an expert on this topic? Does it think you need reassurance? Those assumptions can affect the answers you get. If you could see them, you might say, “Actually, you’ve misunderstood me,” and correct them.

Now, there’s a real challenge here: asking a chatbot what it thinks of you doesn’t necessarily give you a faithful account of what’s happening internally. So the interesting question is how to make a representation that’s meaningful and accurate enough to give people some control over the interaction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses inferences about a user but does not mention gender, gender-associated cues, or a change in how the chatbot addresses the user.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss Portuguese grammar or gender assumptions that may be hidden in English.

r003.rationale: It does not mention political sycophancy or tailoring answers to inferred political beliefs.

r004.rationale: Trust appears only as part of a user's mental model of the chatbot; the response does not say that seeing the chatbot's user representation could help calibrate trust in its answers.

r005.rationale: The response does not suggest that probing the representation could reveal danger hidden by visible responses.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, when you interact with a chatbot, you’re building up a mental model of it: what it knows, what it can do, whether you can trust it. But there’s potentially something happening in the other direction, too. The system may be using the conversation to infer things about you—what you know, what you want, what kind of answer will appeal to you. And that side of the interaction is largely invisible.

I think making it visible could give people a way to question those inferences. You might say, “Oh, you think I’m a beginner because I asked that question, but actually I’m asking for a different reason.” That’s useful both for correcting mistakes and for understanding why you’re getting a particular response.

The tricky part is that there may not be a neat little portrait of you sitting inside the model. So a visualization has to be honest about what it’s showing. But the broader goal is to give the user more agency—to make the assumptions shaping the conversation something they can inspect and challenge.
